case_name: Kramarz v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic Centres
text:
Kramarz et al. v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic Centres et

al.

[Indexed as: Kramarz v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic

Centres]

87 O.R. (3d) 120

Ontario Superior Court of Justice,

Lederer J.

August 29, 2007

Limitations -- Trusts and trustees -- Transition provisions of new Limitations Act not applying to action for damages pursuant to
s. 61(1)
of
Family Law Act
which was commenced more than two years after deceased's 2003 death -- Action being governed by two-year limitation period in
s. 38(3)
of
Trustee Act
-- Section 38(3) of Trustee Act being listed in Schedule to new Limitations Act -- Section 24(4) of new Act not applying as s. 38(3) limitation period is not "former limitation period" -- Section 24(5) of new Act not applying as s. 38(3) limitation period is not limitation period under new Act -- Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, s. 61(1) --
Limitations Act, 2002, S.O. 2002, c. 24, Sched. B, ss. 19(1)
,
24(4)
,
24(5)
-- Trustee Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. T.23, s. 38(3).
The plaintiffs brought an action for damages pursuant to
s. 61(1)
of the
Family Law Act
. The deceased family member died in June 2003. The action was commenced in December 2005, more than two-and-a-half years after the death. The derivative nature of actions brought under the Family Law Act determines that the two-year limitation imposed by
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
applies to these [page121] actions. The action was not brought within two years of the family member's death. The defendants brought a motion to dismiss the action on the basis that it was out of time.
Held, the motion should be granted.
The transition provisions of the
Limitations Act, 2002
(the "new Act") did not apply. Section 19(1) of the new Act provides that a limitation period set out in or under another Act that applies to a claim to which the new Act applies is of no effect unless the provision establishing it is listed in the Schedule to the new Act.
Section 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
is listed in the Schedule. The s. 38(3) limitation period is not a "former limitation period" for the purposes of s. 24(4) of the new Act because, as a result of
s. 19(1)
, it continues in place. In order for
s. 24(5)
to be effective, there must be a limitation period under the new Act that would apply. The limitation period found in s. 38(3) of the Trustee Act is not a limitation period under the new Act. Therefore, s. 24(5) had no application to this case.
MOTION for order dismissing action as statute-barred.

Cases referred to
Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston,
[2007] O.J.   No. 415, 155 A.C.W.S. (3d) 194 , 2007 CarswellOnt 655   (S.C.J.)

1998 CanLII 1523 (ON CA)
, 41 O.R. (3d) 481, [1998] O.J. No.   4367, 167 D.L.R. (4th) 78, 26 E.T.R. (2d) 103, 28 C.P.C. (4th)   389 (C.A.) [Leave to appeal to S.C.C. dismissed [1998]   S.C.C.A. No. 635]; Swain Estate v. Lake of the Woods District   Hospital (1992),
1992 CanLII 7601 (ON CA)
, 9 O.R. (3d) 74, [1992] O.J. No. 1358, 93   D.L.R. (4th) 440, 9 C.P.C. (3d) 169 (C.A.) [Leave to appeal to   S.C.C. refused
[1992] S.C.C.A. No. 467, 164 N.R. 158

[as am.]

15
,

Robert Besunder, for plaintiffs (responding parties).
Robert M. Ben, for defendant (moving party) KMH Cardiology &
Diagnostic Centres.
Elizabeth K.P. Grace and Trevor Shaw, for defendant (moving
party) Dr. Michael M. Abbott, also known as Dr. Meyer Abbott.
[page122]

[
1
] LEDERER J.: -- This is a case about the new
Limitations
Act, 2002, S.O. 2002, c. 24, Sched. B
and how its transition
provisions should be read and implemented.

[
2
] Maria Kramarz died in hospital on June 10, 2003. The
plaintiffs are her spouse, children and minor grandchild. The
defendants are the cardiologist, who performed a stress test on
her on June 2, 2003, and the clinic where the stress test was
undertaken. The Statement of Claim alleges negligence on the
part of the cardiologist and clinic which caused or contributed
to the death.

[
3
] The action was commenced on December 5, 2005. This was
approximately two-and-one-half years after the death of Maria
Kramarz.

[
4
] The plaintiffs obtain the right to sue through the
provisions of the
Family Law Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. F.3, s.
61(1)
, which states:

61(1) If a person is injured or killed by the fault or
neglect of another under circumstances where the person is
entitled to recover damages, or would have been entitled if
not killed, the spouse, as defined in Part III (Support
Obligations), children, grandchildren, parents, grandparents,
brothers and sisters of the person are entitled to recover
their pecuniary loss resulting from the injury or death from
the person from whom the person injured or killed is entitled
to recover or would have been entitled if not killed, and to
maintain an action for the purpose in a court of competent
jurisdiction.

[
5
] This right to sue is derivative of an estate's ability to
commence an action pursuant to the provisions of the
Trustee
Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. T.23
. Section 38(1) of that Act states:

Except in cases of libel and slander, the executor or
administrator of any deceased person may maintain an action
for all torts or injuries to the person or to the property of
the deceased in the same manner and with the same rights and
remedies as the deceased would, if living, have been entitled
to do, and the damages when recovered shall form part of the
personal estate of the deceased; but, if death results from
such injuries, no damages shall be allowed for the death or
the loss of the expectation of life, but this proviso is not
in derogation of any rights conferred by Part V of the
Family
Law Act
.

[
6
] The
Trustee Act
imposes a limitation on actions that may
be brought by an estate. They must be commenced within two
years of the death.
Section 38(3)
of the Trustee Act provides:

38(3) An action under this section shall not be brought
after the expiration of two years from the death of the
deceased.

[
7
] The law is clear. The derivative nature of actions
brought under the
Family Law Act
determines that the two-year
limitation imposed by the
Trustee Act
applies to such actions
(see: Smith Estate v. College of Physicians and Surgeons of
Ontario (1998),
1998 CanLII 1523 (ON CA)
, 41 O.R. (3d) 481, [1998] O.J. No. 4367 (C.A.);
Swain Estate v. Lake of the Woods District Hospital (1992),
1992 CanLII 7601 (ON CA)
, 9
O.R. (3d) 74, [1992] O.J. No. 1358 (C.A.), leave to appeal to
S.C.C. refused,
[1992] S.C.C.A. No. 467, 19 C.P.C. (3d) 25
n;
[page123] and Waschkowski v. Hopkinson Estate (2000),
2000 CanLII 5646 (ON CA)
, 47
O.R. (3d) 370, [2000] O.J. No. 470 (C.A.)).

[
8
] The action was commenced more than two years after the
death. The defendants, relying on rule 21.01 [of the
Rules of
Civil Procedure, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194
], move to have the
action dismissed because it is out of time. Absent the

Limitations Act, 2002
, there is little doubt that the motion
would succeed. The issue is whether the provisions of that
statute allow the action to proceed.

Order

[
9
] The action is dismissed.

[
10
] In interpreting the
Limitations Act, 2002
, it is
important to look beyond a mere reading of the words and
inquire into its overall intent. The transition provisions are
not to be read so that there is no limitation applicable to
actions such as this. The better view is that because the
applicable limitation existed before the Limitations Act, 2002
came into effect, and under the terms of the Act continue, the
transition provisions do not apply. The applicable limitation
is found in the
Trustee Act, s. 38(3)
.

Analysis

[
11
] The analysis of the impact of the
Limitations Act, 2002

deals with the question of transition. How do we deal with the
limited number of situations that arises before the imposition
of the new regime but are still unresolved on the day it
becomes effective?

[
12
] The
Limitations Act, 2002, s. 24
addresses this
question.
Subsection 24(2)
tells us that:

24(2) This section applies to claims based on acts or
omissions that took place before the effective date and in
respect of which no proceeding has been commenced before the
effective date.

[
13
] The Court of Appeal has identified
s. 24
as a transition
provision. It has observed that:

. . . disharmony can be avoided by treating s. 24(5) as a
special provision that applies to a limited number of
transitional situations. . .

(York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd. (2007),

2007 ONCA 49 (CanLII)
, 84 O.R. 414, [2007] O.J. No. 240 (C.A.), at para.
23
)
. . . . .

Section 24(5) is transitory and the situations to which it
applies will run their course.

(York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd., supra,
para.
24
) [page124]

[
14
] All but one of its operative clauses, the ones which
explain how the "limited number of transitional situations"
should be treated (ss. 24(3),
24(4)
, 24(5), and 24(6)), are
conditioned on the presence or absence of a "former limitation
period". (The exception, s. 24(7), deals with claims based on
assault or a sexual assault and is not relevant here.) "Former
limitation period" is defined by s. 24(1) as:

"Former limitation period" means the limitation period that
applied in respect of the claim before the coming into force
of this Act.

[
15
] An understanding of the impact of
s. 24
on this
situation begins with a determination of the meaning behind the
definition of "former limitation period".

[
16
] Counsel for the defendants, the moving parties, says
there is no "former limitation period" apparent in this case.
The limitation contained in the
Trustee Act, s. 38(3)
,continues
to be effective. The
Limitations Act, 2002
indicates the
continued operation of s. 38(3) of the
Trustee Act
. Section
19(1) of the Act states:

19(1) A limitation period set out in or under another Act
that applies to a claim to which this Act applies is of no
effect unless,

(a) the provision establishing it is listed in the
Schedule to this Act; or

(b) the provision establishing it,

(i) is in existence on the day this Act comes into
force, and

(ii) incorporates by reference a provision listed in
the Schedule to this Act.

[
17
] Section 19(1)(a) applies. Section 38(3) is listed in the
Schedule to the Act. Accordingly, counsel submits, it does not
present a "former limitation period" because it continues to
exist. We are not dealing with a past limitation in the face of
a new one. The same limitation continues unaltered. This being
the case, it is argued that
s. 24
has no application. We are
not transitioning from one limitation to another. The
plaintiff's right to sue ended on the second anniversary of the
death of Maria Kramarz.

[
18
] Counsel for the plaintiffs, the responding parties,
takes a different approach. The limitation period found in the

Trustee Act, s. 38(3)
,does fall within the definition of
"former limitation period". It is a limitation that applied
"before the coming into force of this Act". There is no need
to go further. In these circumstances, he says, it becomes
necessary to consider whether
s. 24(4)
of the
Limitations Act,
2002
applies. Section 24(4) states:

24(4) If the former limitation period did not expire before
the effective date and if no limitation period under this Act
would apply were the claim based [page125] on an act or
omission that took place on or after the effective date,
there is no limitation period.

[
19
] This argument is based on the premise that there is a
former limitation period (the limitation found in the
Trustee
Act, s. 38(3)
). The facts establish that it had not expired as
of the effective date. The remaining condition for the
application of
s. 24(4)
is the question of whether there is a
"limitation period under this Act" that would apply. Is the
limitation in the Trustee Act, s. 38(3), a "limitation period
under this Act"? Is the fact that it is included on the
Schedule enough to find that it satisfies this condition? This
court has held that it is not (see: Bikur Cholim Jewish
Volunteer Services v. Langston,
[2007] O.J. No. 415, 2007
CarswellOnt 655 (S.C.J.)
). In that case, the court was dealing
with
s. 24(6)
of the
Limitations Act, 2002
, but the issue is
the same. The court refers to [Driedger on the Construction of
Statutes, 3rd ed. (Markham, Ont.: Butterworths, 1994) by Ruth
Sullivan], p. 279:

. . . where, the author states, that materials set out in a
schedule may be given the force of law by being incorporated
into the Act to which they are appended. Generally, says
Driedger, the incorporation is obvious and explicit. Even if
such Schedule is not incorporated, says Driedger, it may be
relied on in interpreting the Act.

(Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston, supra, at
para. 20)

[
20
] The court determined that the
Trustee Act
had not been
incorporated into the
Limitations Act, 2002
:

However, a limitation period under another Act, that is
s.
38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
, is not, by definition, a limitation
period under the new Limitations Act. Therefore, the answer
to the question as to whether a limitation period under the
new Act would apply if the claim was based on an act or
omission that took place after the effective date is "no".

(Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston, supra, at
para. 27)

[
21
] On this basis, the answer is "no" in this case, as well.
This means that all the conditions necessary for the
application of
s. 24(4)
are met. Pursuant to its wording,
counsel says, "there is no limitation period". The plaintiffs
are free to continue their action.

[
22
] Counsel for the defendant, the moving party, have a
response to this. While counsel for the plaintiff submits that
the plain meaning of the words suggests that there is no
limitation period, the other side says the matter should not
stop with the reading of the subsection. Counsel for the moving
parties points to
s. 19(4)
of the
Limitations Act, 2002
, which
states: [page126]

19(4) If there is a conflict between a limitation period
established by a provision referred to in subsection (1) and
one established by another provision of this Act, the
limitation period established by the provision referred to in
subsection (1) prevails.

[
23
] As noted, subsection (1) includes the limitation period
found in the
Trustee Act
. Counsel submits that there is a
limitation period provided by "any other provision of this
Act". This is the imposition of "no limitation period" found in

s. 24(4)
. The two are in conflict (no limitation period versus
a two-year limitation from the death). Pursuant to
s. 19(4)
of
the
Limitations Act, 2002
, the conflict is resolved by giving
precedence to the Act referred to in s. 19(1). This is the
Trustee Act. On this basis, counsel for the defendants says the
two-year limitation continues to apply and the action being
considered is out of time.

[
24
] The question is how to resolve the two different
approaches proposed. Counsel for the plaintiffs, the responding
parties, asks for a narrow reading of the words found in the

Limitations Act, 2002
. He points out that there was a
limitation in place before the coming into force of the new
Act. He noted the fact that it continues in place is not
referred to in the legislation and is therefore of no moment in
dealing with this situation. "No limitation period" means that
there is no limitation to conflict with the
Trustee Act, s.
38(3)
and, accordingly, there is nothing preventing the action
from continuing.

[
25
] The defendants, the moving parties, say we must do more
than read these words. We need to examine the Act as a whole to
determine its overall intent. In York Condominium Corp. No. 382
v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd., supra, the interpretation of the
transition provisions of the
Limitations Act, 2002
was
considered. The Court of Appeal observed [at para. 13]:

Having determined the ordinary meaning, the court must go on
to consider the context of the provision, the purpose and
scheme of the legislation as well as the consequences of
adopting the ordinary meaning and any other relevant
indicators of legislative meaning. If, after understanding
this analysis, the words of the provision are reasonably
capable of more than one meaning, a real ambiguity exists.
Bell ExpressVu, [Limited Partnership v. Rex,
2002 SCC 42 (CanLII)
, [2002] 2 S.C.R.
559].

The court must adopt an interpretation that best fulfills
the objects of the legislation.

(York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd., supra,
paras.
13-14
)

[
26
] The Court of Appeal also noted:

Driedger articulates the common-sense proposition that
effect should be given to the ordinary meaning of a
legislative provision unless there is good reason not to do
so. The court is therefore required to consider the purpose
[page127] and scheme of the legislation, the consequences of
adopting the ordinary meaning and all the relevant
indicators of legislative meaning. In light of these
additional considerations the court may adopt an
interpretation that modifies or rejects the ordinary meaning
provided that the words can bear the proposed alternative
meaning.

(York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd., supra,
at para.
26
)

[
27
] With this in mind, the court stated:

The purpose of the [
Limitations Act, 2002
] as a whole is to
balance the right to access to justice by bringing a lawsuit
with the right to certainty and finality in the organization
of one's affairs.
(York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v. Jay-M Holdings Ltd., supra,
at para.
32
)

[
28
] The simple reading of the words, as proposed by counsel
for the plaintiffs, takes us to a peculiar place: the idea that
there is no limitation period which applies to this situation.
This is inconsistent with the overall structure and intent of
the legislation.

[
29
] For the few cases this approach would govern, there
would be no limitation. The potential plaintiffs would obtain
new rights. They could sue forever. This is different from the
treatment given to actions that arose before and after the
actions affected by the transition provisions. In those
situations, prospective plaintiffs would be constrained by the
two-year limitation period found in the
Trustee Act, s. 38(1)
.

[
30
]
Section 15
of the
Limitations Act, 2002
put in place an
"ultimate limitation period" of 15 years from the date of
the act or omission on which the claim is based. It applies
where the limitation period established by any other section of
the Limitations Act, 2002 has not expired. Counsel for the
plaintiff's submission is based on the premise that there is no
limitation period. This is why the conflict provision of
s.
19(4)
, in his view, is not effective. In respect of s. 15, it
follows there would be no limitation period to "expire". Hence,
s. 15 would not apply in this case and the ability to sue would
never end.

[
31
] In this situation, it is difficult to see how the
balance the Act strives to put in place is accomplished. There
would never be finality for the defendants to these claims.

[
32
] The better view is that expressed on behalf of the
defendants. In examining the definition of "former limitation
period", it would be wrong to ignore the impact of the use of
the word "former" in the phrase being defined. "Former" in its
ordinary meaning refers to something in the past. In the
Concise Oxford Dictionary, 11th Edition (Revised), "former" is
defined as: "of or occurring in the past". Understood in this
way, the limitation [page128] period in the
Trustee Act
is not
a "former limitation period" because as a result of
s. 19(1)
of
the
Limitations Act, 2002
it continues in place. We are not
transitioning from one regime to another. The Trustee Act did
and does apply. It is not "of. . . the past". The rights of the
plaintiffs have not and will not change. The idea that for a
brief period they have changed so that there is no applicable
limitation period is not demonstrated by any policy, intention
or words found in or derived from the legislation. Accordingly,
the action is out of time.

[
33
] This does not deal with the submissions that have been
made, on behalf of the defendants, which rely on
s. 24(5)
of
the
Limitations Act, 2002
. It states:

24(5) If the former limitation period did not expire before
the effective date and if a limitation period under this act
would apply were the claim based on an act or omission that
took place on or after the effective date, the following
rules apply:

1. If the claim was not discovered before the effective
date, this Act applies as if the act or omission had
taken place on the effective date.

2. If the claim was discovered before the effective date
the former limitation applies.

(Emphasis added)

[
34
] In order for this subsection to be effective, there must
be a limitation period under the Limitation Act, 2002 that
would apply. This is what separates
s. 24(5)
from
s. 24(4)
. As
noted above, this court in York Condominium Corp. No. 382 v.
Jay-M Holdings Ltd., supra, determined that the limitation
period found in the
Trustee Act, s. 38(3)
, is not a limitation
period under the
Limitations Act, 2002
. I see no reason to make
a different determination here.

[
35
] In Sullivan and Driedger on the Construction of
Statutes, 4th ed. (Markham, Ont.: Butterworths, 2002), the
following comments are made with reference to the reasons of
Iacobucci J. in the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in
British Columbia (Attorney General) v. Canada (Attorney
General),
1994 CanLII 81 (SCC)
, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 41, [1994] S.C.J. No. 35, at para.

118
:

He relied in particular on the Manitoba Court of Appeal's
reasons for a judgment in Winnipeg v. Winnipeg Electric
Railway Co.,
1921 CanLII 378 (MB CA)
, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 282 (Man. C.A.), at p. 306,
where Fullerton J.A. wrote:

. . . in order to make an agreement scheduled to an Act a
part of the Act itself, it is not sufficient to find the
words in the statute merely confirming and validating the
agreement: you must find words from which the intention can
be inferred. [page129]

Iacobucci J. added [at paras. 118 and 121]:

Like the Court of Appeal, I do not regard this statement as
meaning that a scheduled agreement will have statutory force
only if that intention is made express in a particular
provision, e.g. "the agreement is hereby confirmed, ratified
and endowed with statutory force". . . . Rather, all of the
tools of statutory interpretation can be called in aid to
determine whether incorporation is intended. . . . I do
believe, however, that simple "ratification" or
"confirmation" of a scheduled agreement, without more, is
equivocal in terms of the required legislative intention.

. . . . .

. . . The Dominion Act simply confirms and ratifies the
Dunsmuir Agreement...

(Sullivan and Driedger on the Construction of Statutes, pp.
318-319)

[
36
] In this case, the scheduling of the
Trustee Act, s.
38(3)
, is a validation of the limitation provisions listed.
There is no language expressed or intention demonstrated to
incorporate these provisions into the
Limitations Act, 2002
.

[
37
] Accti2ingly, s. 24(5) has no application to this case.

[
38
] The impact of this is to demonstrate that, if I am wrong
in my finding as to the meaning of the definition of "former
limitation period", then it is
s. 24(4)
of the
Limitations Act,
2002
that applies. There would, in those circumstances, be "no
limitation period". If this were the case, I would still find
that the action is out of time pursuant to the limitation
period found in the
Trustee Act, s. 38(3)
. As suggested above,
any inquiry into the intention of the Limitations Act, 2002
cannot sustain the idea that there is no limitation period that
constrains the plaintiff's right to sue. The interpretation
utilized, on behalf of the defendants, to the effect that this
reference still allows for reliance on
s. 19(4)
of the
Limitations Act, 2002 takes us, in turn, to the difference
between "no limitation period" and the two-year limitation
period found within the
Trustee Act
. It resolves the conflict
in favour of the Trustee Act. The action would still be out of
time.

[
39
] This still does not finally resolve the matter. The

Limitations Act, 2002
is clear in its intention to allow
actions in favour of minors to continue until they are of age.

[
40
]
Section 19(5)
of the
Limitations Act, 2002
states:

19(5) Sections 6, 7 and 11 apply, with necessary
modifications, to a limitation period established by the
provision referred to in subsection (1).

[
41
] In turn,
s. 6
, to which
s. 19(5)
refers, states:

6. The limitation period established by section 4 does not
run during any time in which the person with the claim,

(a) is a minor; and

(b) is not represented by a litigation guardian in
relation to the claim. [page130]

[
42
] Section 6 applies to limitations made effective by s.
19(1). The limitations that apply to claims of minors who are
unrepresented by a litigation guardian are extended while they
remain minor. In this case, the grandchild of Maria Kramarz
sued by his litigation guardian. The limitation period
continued to run. This action is also out of time.

Costs

[
43
] There were no submissions made as to costs. If the
parties are unable to agree, I will consider submissions, in
writing, made on the following terms: from the defendants, the
moving parties, within 15 days of the issuance of these reasons
and from the plaintiffs, the responding parties, within ten
days thereafter. Such submissions are to be no longer than
three pages, in addition to any cost outline that may be
provided.

Motion granted.
